Frequencies and mosaic plots

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/frequencies-and-mosaic.Rmd
frequencies-and-mosaic.Rmd

A transition network describes how the actors move between codes, but not how often each code occurs in the first place. The two kinds of information are read together. A transition out of a rare code can carry a high probability on a handful of events, and a code that dominates one actor’s activity shapes the edges of the whole network. In a heterogeneous network the frequencies have a further role: they show how each actor divides its activity over its own codes, which is the first description of the division of labor between a human and an AI.

This guide covers two summaries that precede and accompany the network. The frequency tables and plots give the distribution of the codes within each actor and over the whole interaction. The mosaic plot gives the joint distribution of consecutive codes, with each cell shaded by how far its count departs from the count expected if the next code did not depend on the current one.

library(htna)

Data

human_ai holds 429 sessions of human-AI pair programming; each row is one coded event.

  • Session: session_id.
  • Code: code; six human and six AI codes.
  • Actor type: actor_type, "Human" or "AI".
  • Order: order_in_session.

The frequency summaries use the relative network. The mosaic tests counts, so it needs the network of transition counts (method = "frequency").

data(human_ai)
net <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type")
net_counts <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type",
                         method = "frequency")

How does each actor divide its activity?

frequencies_htna() counts every code and reports it under its actor, with its share of that actor’s events. The shares sum to one within each actor.

frequencies_htna(net)
#>    group     state count proportion
#> 1     AI   Execute  3258     0.3810
#> 2  Human   Request  3104     0.2875
#> 3  Human   Specify  2920     0.2705
#> 4     AI       Ask  2416     0.2825
#> 5  Human Frustrate  1829     0.1694
#> 6     AI      Plan  1620     0.1895
#> 7  Human     Check  1298     0.1202
#> 8  Human   Inquire   853     0.0790
#> 9  Human    Refine   792     0.0734
#> 10    AI    Report   705     0.0824
#> 11    AI  Delegate   295     0.0345
#> 12    AI    Repair   257     0.0301

The AI’s activity is concentrated: executions are 38.1% of its events and asks 28.3%, while delegations (3.45%) and repairs (3.01%) are rare. The human’s activity is spread over requests (28.8%), specifications (27.1%) and expressions of frustration (16.9%). Edges out of Delegate and Repair rest on fewer than 300 events each and have wider intervals than edges out of Execute (see Model assessment).

The treemap shows the same table, one panel per actor, with each tile’s area proportional to the code’s share of its actor.

plot_frequencies_htna(net)

Which codes dominate the interaction as a whole?

state_frequencies_htna() gives the pooled table: each code’s share of all events, whichever actor produced it.

state_frequencies_htna(net)
#>        state count proportion
#> 1    Execute  3258     0.1684
#> 2    Request  3104     0.1604
#> 3    Specify  2920     0.1509
#> 4        Ask  2416     0.1249
#> 5  Frustrate  1829     0.0945
#> 6       Plan  1620     0.0837
#> 7      Check  1298     0.0671
#> 8    Inquire   853     0.0441
#> 9     Refine   792     0.0409
#> 10    Report   705     0.0364
#> 11  Delegate   295     0.0152
#> 12    Repair   257     0.0133

Pooled over both actors, the AI’s executions (16.8% of all events) and the human’s requests (16.0%) and specifications (15.1%) together make up almost half of the interaction. The bar view puts both actors on one axis, sorted by count and coloured by actor, for this comparison across actors.

plot_frequencies_htna(net, view = "bars")

Because the two actors produce different numbers of events, the faceted view, with a separate axis per actor, is the better display when the question is the profile within each actor.

plot_frequencies_htna(net, view = "facet")

Which transitions occur more often than chance?

mosaic_plot_htna() draws the table of consecutive codes, source codes in columns and target codes stacked within them. The width of a column is the share of transitions from that code and the height of a tile the share of its target, so the area of a tile is the share of that transition. Each tile is shaded by its standardised residual against independence of source and target: blue tiles are transitions that occur more often than independence predicts, red tiles less often. The residuals are estimated by permutation (500 permutations by default), which needs no large-sample approximation; residuals = "asymptotic" gives the closed-form chi-square residuals instead. The axis labels are coloured by actor. Clipping the colour scale to plus or minus 4 keeps a few extreme cells from washing out the rest.

mosaic_plot_htna(net_counts, range = c(-4, 4), seed = 1L)

The mosaic is the cell-level counterpart of the turn-taking templates of the Sequences and patterns guide, where handovers between the actors occur 1.22 to 1.28 times as often as independence predicts; here each tile shows which specific pair of codes carries that excess. Reading the network together with the mosaic distinguishes a strong edge that is strong because its target is common from one that is strong because the source specifically leads to it.

Which summary to use

Question Function
How does each actor divide its activity over its codes? frequencies_htna(), plot_frequencies_htna()
Which codes dominate the whole interaction? state_frequencies_htna(), plot_frequencies_htna(view = "bars")
Within-actor profiles when the actors differ in volume plot_frequencies_htna(view = "facet")
Which consecutive pairs occur more or less often than chance? mosaic_plot_htna() on a frequency network
